lead: The Stern-Gerlach experiment fires silver atoms through a non-uniform magnetic field. Two spots appear, not a continuous smear: spin along that axis is quantised. Rotate the magnet and the beam splits again, while the earlier result is wiped out. That wiping out is measurement disturbance, the physical face of the uncertainty principle. The Robertson relation turns it into an inequality about spreads. Spin measurement, NMR and spin qubits rest on this.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.5 on projective measurement and the Born rule, plus commutators from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Silver atoms in a non-uniform field

blocks.text: An oven heats silver until atoms evaporate. A slit collimates them into a beam that passes between magnet poles and lands on a screen. The magnet is shaped so the field is stronger near one pole: the field is non-uniform along z.

A silver atom has 47 electrons. Forty-six fill closed shells with no net angular momentum. The forty-seventh sits in a 5s orbital with zero orbital angular momentum. So the atom's magnetic moment comes almost entirely from that electron's spin. Write μ for magnetic moment and S for spin. Then μ = -g(e/2m)S, where e is the electron charge magnitude in coulombs, m is the electron mass in kilograms, and g ≈ 2 (more precisely 2.0023) is the electron spin g-factor, a dimensionless number.

A uniform field twists the magnetic moment but exerts zero net force. A non-uniform field also pushes. The force along z is proportional to μ_z, and μ_z is proportional to S_z. Classically S_z could take any value, so the beam would spread into a continuous band. Quantum mechanics allows only S_z = +ħ/2 or S_z = -ħ/2, where ħ = h/2π ≈ 1.055×10⁻³⁴ J·s is the reduced Planck constant. So the band becomes two spots.

blocks.where: F_z is the force on one atom along z in newtons; μ_z is the z-component of its magnetic moment in A·m² (or J/T); dB/dz is the field gradient along z in tesla per metre.

blocks.text: Take z toward the upper spot and the field stronger at the lower pole (dB/dz < 0). Then S_z = +ħ/2 gives μ_z < 0 and a force toward +z, so the upper spot is spin-up along z.

items: Heat silver in an oven; atoms escape through a hole.
Pass it through a magnet whose field points along z and changes strength along z.
Record the landing positions: two spots, symmetric about the straight-through line.

blocks.text: First run: one magnet along z. Two spots. Block the lower spot and send only the upper beam into a second magnet along z. Only one spot appears, in the upper position. A second measurement of S_z gives the same answer. After the first measurement the atom is in the spin-up state along z.

Second run: keep the z-up beam but rotate the second magnet along x. The single beam splits into two equal beams. An atom with definite S_z has no definite S_x. Each x outcome has probability 1/2, and the state after the second magnet is spin-up or spin-down along x. The old z information is gone.

Third run: take one x beam and pass it through a magnet along z. Two equal beams appear again. Nothing of the earlier z measurement survives. Each magnet measures one axis and randomises the others. This is projective measurement, described in Chapter 2.5.

blocks.where: |↑_z⟩ is the state with S_z = +ħ/2; |↑_x⟩ and |↓_x⟩ are the states with S_x = +ħ/2 and -ħ/2; the factor 1/√2 makes the total probability equal to 1.

items: A z magnet on a fresh beam: half exits each port.
The upper z beam into an x magnet: half exits each x port.
As fractions of the original beam: 1/2 exits each z port, then 1/4 exits each x port.
The relative phase between the two terms does not change these probabilities, but decides interference if the beams are recombined.

blocks.text: Let A and B be two observables, Hermitian operators, and let the system be in any state. The spread of A is ΔA = √(⟨A²⟩ − ⟨A⟩²), the standard deviation of many measurements on identical copies. Robertson's inequality relates the two spreads.

blocks.where: ΔA and ΔB are the standard deviations of A and B in the given state; [A,B] = AB − BA is the commutator; ⟨·⟩ is the expectation value in that state. If [A,B] = 0, the bound is zero and both observables can be sharp together.

blocks.text: For spin, [S_x,S_y] = iħS_z and cyclic partners. Substitute: ΔS_x ΔS_y ≥ (ħ/2)|⟨S_z⟩|. A state with sharp S_z cannot have sharp S_x or S_y. For the spin-up state along z, ΔS_x = ħ/2 and ΔS_y = ħ/2, so the product is ħ²/4. The bound is (ħ/2)(ħ/2) = ħ²/4, so the inequality is exact there, not slack.

The same logic with [x,p] = iħ gives Δx Δp ≥ ħ/2, where x is position in metres and p is momentum in kg·m/s. The spread is a property of the state, not of a clumsy apparatus. A perfect instrument still cannot prepare a state with both values sharp. This matters for entanglement: in an entangled pair the outcomes are correlated along whichever axis is measured. A measurement on one part tells you what a measurement on the other part along that same axis will give; it does not change the other part, and it says nothing about other axes.

figure.caption: Silver atoms leave the oven, pass one non-uniform magnet along z, and land as two spots: one spin-up beam and one spin-down beam. No atoms land in the middle.

spec.title: Stern-Gerlach
spec.aria: Silver atoms pass an inhomogeneous magnet and split into two spin beams on a screen.

examples.question: A silver atom beam passes a Stern-Gerlach magnet along z. (a) What fraction exits each z port? (b) The upper z beam enters an x magnet. What fraction of the original beam exits each x port? (c) For a state with ΔS_x = ħ/2 and ⟨S_z⟩ = ħ/2, find the minimum ΔS_y.
steps: (a) No preferred spin axis, so equal z outcomes: 1/2 up, 1/2 down.
(b) Upper z beam is |↑_z⟩ = (|↑_x⟩ + |↓_x⟩)/√2, so each x outcome has probability 1/2. It is 1/2 of original, so each x port carries (1/2)(1/2)=1/4.
(c) Use [S_x,S_y]=iħS_z: ΔS_x ΔS_y ≥ (ħ/2)|⟨S_z⟩|. Put in values: (ħ/2)ΔS_y ≥ ħ²/4, so ΔS_y ≥ ħ/2 ≈ 5.27×10⁻³⁵ J·s.
examples.answer: Each z port gets 1/2, each x port 1/4 of the original beam, and minimum ΔS_y = ħ/2.

traps: Adding probabilities across axes. Each x port holds 1/4 of the original, not 1/2.
Expecting the second z magnet to split the upper beam. Undisturbed, it gives one spot.
Treating the uncertainty relation as instrument noise. ΔA belongs to the state.
Dropping ½ or ħ in ΔS_x ΔS_y ≥ (ħ/2)|⟨S_z⟩|.
Confusing ΔA with the eigenvalue gap. For spin-½ the gap is ħ but ΔS_x ≤ ħ/2.

quiz.q: What pattern appears on the screen after one z magnet?
quiz.a: Two spots of equal strength, symmetric about the straight-through line, for S_z = +ħ/2 and -ħ/2. No atoms land between them.

quiz.q: Why does a uniform field fail to split the beam?
quiz.a: A uniform field exerts torque but zero net force, since force depends on the field gradient. No gradient means no separation by spin.

quiz.q: A beam passes a z magnet, the upper beam an x magnet, and the upper x beam a further z magnet. What fraction of the original beam exits each port of the last magnet?
quiz.a: First z gives 1/2 up. x magnet splits that into 1/4 and 1/4. Upper x beam is 1/4 of original and splits equally in final z: (1/2)(1/4)=1/8 at each port.

quiz.q: For a state with ΔS_x = ħ/2 and ⟨S_z⟩ = 0, what lower bound on ΔS_y?
quiz.a: ΔS_x ΔS_y ≥ (ħ/2)|⟨S_z⟩| = 0. No positive bound; ΔS_y can be anything allowed. Such a state is not an S_z eigenstate.

quiz.q: Explain why Robertson relation is about the state, not instrument quality.
quiz.a: ΔA, ΔB are standard deviations from the state's amplitudes, not measurement errors. If operators don't commute, no state has both spreads zero, so ideal measurements on identical copies must scatter in at least one. Better apparatus reduces technical noise only.

quiz.q: State the Robertson uncertainty relation and define symbols.
quiz.a: ΔA ΔB ≥ ½|⟨[A,B]⟩|, where A, B are Hermitian operators, [A,B]=AB−BA is the commutator, ⟨·⟩ is expectation value in the state, and ΔA=√(⟨A²⟩−⟨A⟩²) is the standard deviation.

quiz.q: For the S_z = +ħ/2 eigenstate, compute ΔS_x ΔS_y and compare with the bound.
quiz.a: Here ⟨S_x⟩=0, ⟨S_x²⟩=ħ²/4, so ΔS_x=ħ/2; likewise ΔS_y=ħ/2. Product = ħ²/4. Bound = (ħ/2)|⟨S_z⟩| = (ħ/2)(ħ/2)=ħ²/4. Product equals bound: a minimum-uncertainty state.

beyond: Not for the exam. Spin qubits in silicon and nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond use exactly these spin measurements, so Stern-Gerlach is an engineering diagram, not just history. Modern security proofs for quantum key distribution use entropic uncertainty relations, which bound an eavesdropper's knowledge. The Robertson bound also generalises to the Schrödinger form, which adds a covariance term and is tighter whenever that covariance is nonzero, for pure as well as mixed states. Search next for entropic uncertainty relations and spin-qubit readout.
